transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-05
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Nadia Patel (HorizonCare Head of ML), Tom Briggs (HorizonCare Staff SWE), Ellen Wu (HorizonCare Data Eng), Jacob Lee (Product)

Summary (auto): Discussed embedding dimensions, throughput constraints, vector DB integration and tradeoffs between hosted/dedicated/private for PHI. Action items captured.

[00:00] Maya (AE): All right everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Diego our solutions engineer. Can we do quick intros from HorizonCare?
[00:10] Nadia: Yeah hi I'm Nadia, head of ML at HorizonCare. We own the search and recommendations stack across clinical docs.
[00:16] Tom: Tom here, infra and backend. We manage ingestion pipelines and the vector DB cluster.
[00:20] Ellen: Ellen, data engineering, I own the ETL and embeddings batch jobs.
[00:24] Jacob: Jacob from product, helping prioritize use-cases.
[00:28] Diego (SE): Awesome. Quick agenda: understand current system, volume/throughput targets, embedding dims and model, and then map to hosted/dedicated/private options and a pilot plan. Sound good?
[00:36] Nadia: Yup. To start, we currently use a home-grown vector store backed by OpenSearch + a Faiss-style ANN offline. It's been a pain for scaling but cheaper. We're evaluating Redwood to replace or augment the ANN and handle reranking.
[00:48] Tom: For numbers: ingest about 20M docs, nightly re-embed run. QPS target for search is spiky: 1k sustained with 2k spikes for events. Latency SLO for first-pass retrieval should be <= 120ms, end-to-end rerank occasionally allowed up to 400ms for complex queries.
[01:06] Diego: Good context. Is the data PHI? Any residency or compliance needs?
[01:10] Nadia: Yes some records are PHI. We're US-only for now. SOC2 is required and we need KMS integration; ideally customer-managed keys.
[01:18] Maya: Noted. Redwood supports KMS/HSM and private deployments. We can provide SOC2 docs — I'll send them after.
[01:24] Ellen: Also curious on how you handle prefix/KV cache with long clinical notes — we hit long sequences often.
[01:30] Diego: We do prefix and KV caching; for long contexts we try to shard the query or use windowing. The cache reduces repeated token computation significantly for conversation-style prompts, less for one-off long doc queries.
[01:44] Tom: For vector DB, we're currently storing 1024-d vectors from an internal embedder; we see space and latency issues. Thinking of switching to 1536 dims for downstream accuracy — but worried about storage and ANN index performance. Any recommendations?
[01:56] Diego: There's a tradeoff. 1536 typically gives a bump on semantic recall, but storage + ANN probing costs go up ~50%. For ANN indexes (HNSW) you'll see higher memory and slightly slower coarse recall times, but you can tune beam and ef parameters. Redwood's routing can fall back to smaller quantized variants for hot paths.
[02:14] Nadia: Can you quantify the per-embedding unit cost across hosted vs dedicated? We need to model monthly spend with 20M vectors and 1.5k QPS.
[02:22] Maya: We'll share an example calc — but short answer: hosted is simplest for quick win, but at your sustained QPS and vector storage you'll probably save substantially by dedicated reserved capacity where we lock in GPU pools and lower per-token/embedding price. We'll send a side-by-side.
[02:38] Jacob: Is dedicated compatible with VPC and our key management needs?
[02:42] Maya: Yes, dedicated supports VPC peering and customer-managed KMS; private deployment (on-prem or VPC-private control plane) is also an option for stricter controls.
[02:52] Ellen: On reranking — we want BM25 first-pass + ANN recall (top 200) then neural rerank with cross-encoder. How would Redwood support that pipeline?
[03:00] Diego: Common pattern: do BM25 to surface candidates, then ANN to expand recall, use a bi-encoder for cheap scoring and then cross-encoder for final rerank on the top N (like 50-200). Redwood supports endpoint chaining; you can run model A for embedding + recall, then stream hits into a heavier rerank model within the same request flow or as a second call with low-latency routing.
[03:24] Tom: Latency is a concern if we do cross-encoder for every user query. We'll likely only rerank top 50. Can Redwood guarantee cold-start latency on rerank models?
[03:33] Diego: We provide latency SLOs per deployment type; dedicated gives tighter guarantees. We also support warmed model instances and per-route min-replicas to avoid cold starts. There's a tradeoff with cost; we can show a canary pattern where heavy rerank runs in background and UX uses first-pass results until rerank completes.
[03:52] Nadia: On throughput benchmarks — what's realistic for 1536-d bi-encoder at 1k qps?
[03:58] Diego: Depends on quantization and batching. With INT8 quantized model and continuous batching on a good A100-style pool, you can hit ~1k qps for small bi-encoder pairs if you batch and use a dedicated pool. But for cross-encoders it's much lower — those are heavier. We'll run a quick bench to approximate your workload.
[04:18] Ellen: How about updating vectors — we have nightly upserts and mid-day corrections. How does Redwood handle high write churn?
[04:25] Maya: We support high write throughput with configurable ingestion pipelines. For Dedicated, you can allocate dedicated insert throughput and we support incremental index rebuilds/vectors upsert. If you're doing heavy real-time inserts, Private or Dedicated gives more control.
[04:38] Tom: Any specifics on vector compression/quantization to save storage? We used productized PQ before but it affected recall on edge cases.
[04:44] Diego: Quantization options: INT8, FP16, PQ; Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per-model and workload. For clinical docs, we'd likely recommend hybrid: keep top-k vectors in higher precision for critical records and PQ the rest, or apply asymmetric quantization.
[05:00] Jacob: What's the migration strategy from our OpenSearch + Faiss setup? Minimal downtime is key.
[05:06] Maya: Typical path: export a sample (we asked for 1k sample vectors earlier), run side-by-side evals on recall/cost, do a pilot with a shadow traffic run for a subset of queries, then gradual cutover. For low-risk, keep BM25 as a fallback route.
[05:20] Nadia: Can you walk us through an example of a hybrid search config — I want to write it down.
[05:26] Diego: Sure: query => BM25 top 100 -> ANN recall top 800 (configured ef/beam to tune speed) -> bi-encoder re-score top 200 -> cross-encoder final re-rank top 50. Use caching for common queries and prefix caching for conversational prompts. The routing policy pins rerank to dedicated nodes with higher-memory GPUs.
[05:48] Tom: How are embeddings charged in hosted? It's per-vector-store unit or per-embedding compute? We need clarity for cost modeling.
[05:56] Maya: Hosted usually charges per-embedding unit (ingest) and per-token for generation/other models. Storage for vectors is billed separately or included depending on plan; we'll share precise line items. For dedicated, you typically have reserved capacity fees plus lower per-usage cost.
[06:12] Ellen: A quick clarification: if we want private deployment inside our AWS account, do we still get Redwood support and console?
[06:18] Maya: Yes, you get a private control plane that can be customer-managed; we provide the console and support, but networking and some infra footprint lives in your account.
[06:26] Nadia: Security — do you support SAML SSO for our teams and RBAC for dataset access?
[06:31] Maya: Yes, SAML, SCIM provisioning for users, and granular RBAC for datasets and model routes. Audit logs and retention configurable for compliance.
[06:42] Jacob: Back to performance — can you explain continuous batching behavior? We worry about latency spikes for small, interactive queries.
[06:48] Diego: Continuous batching will aggregate requests over a short window; you can set max latency thresholds. For interactive queries we recommend small max-batch windows and route interactive paths to low-latency pools, while background high-throughput paths use larger batches for efficiency.
[07:04] Ellen: Any known issues with long clinical notes and KV cache misuse — we saw cache thrash on prior systems.
[07:10] Diego: Thrashed caches usually happen when sequence uniqueness is high. We recommend pre-hashing or chunking long docs and keeping a normalized prefix for repeated queries. Also monitor cache hit ratio in Redwood Console; Optimize will suggest chunk sizes.
[07:26] Maya: Quick question — are you considering switching embedding model families, or staying with internal embedder?
[07:30] Nadia: We're exploring switching to a public 1536 model, but worried about recalibrating downstream thresholds. Also retraining some rerankers may be needed.
[07:38] Diego: We can help with an eval harness to compare 1024 vs 1536 on your dataset and compute estimated uplift and storage delta.
[07:46] Tom: On the ANN side, do you manage indexes or is that customer-managed?
[07:50] Maya: For hosted/dedicated, Redwood manages index lifecycle but you control configs and can trigger rebuilds. For private/self-hosted options, you might manage indexes but Redwood provides orchestration tools.
[08:02] Ellen: Can you show us a sample perf trace or dashboard?
[08:06] Diego: I'll attach a sample perf trace and a screenshot of per-route latency breakdown after the call.
[08:12] Nadia: For SLA terms, what uptime do you guarantee for dedicated?
[08:16] Maya: Typical dedicated SLAs are in the 99.9%+ range for uptime with latency targets defined per route. We can go over contract specifics with your procurement team.
[08:26] Jacob: Any customers in healthcare you can reference?
[08:29] Maya: We have a couple of customers in regulated industries — I'll include anonymized case studies and security contacts.
[08:36] Tom: A bit more technical: how do you handle vector sharding and routing for multi-tenant datasets? We want some tenants isolated for privacy.
[08:44] Diego: For dedicated, you can pin tenants to specific GPU pools and have namespace separation; private gives stronger isolation. Sharding is transparent — routing is by namespace and we can route particular datasets to specific index shards for locality.
[09:00] Ellen: Our ingestion cadence — nightly with small mid-day inserts. Will that cause heavy rebuilds?
[09:06] Diego: Incremental upserts with lazy rebuilds are possible; we won't rebuild entire index for small inserts. For big batched rebuilds we schedule out of peak hours. We'll review your cadence and recommend settings.
[09:18] Nadia: Can Redwood attach to our existing vector DB (we already have some Faiss clusters)? Maybe use Redwood for model serving and rerank only.
[09:26] Maya: Yes, hybrid deployments are common — you can continue using existing ANN and call Redwood for embedding generation and rerank models. Or we can ingest vectors from your DB into Redwood for unified tooling.
[09:38] Tom: For experimentation we want A/B tests of rerankers. Does Redwood support traffic splitting?
[09:43] Diego: Yes, we support canary and A/B rollouts, per-route splitting, and evaluation hooks to compare metrics like recall@k and latency.
[09:50] Jacob: Great. Any gotchas on cold-starts for cross-encoder when traffic patterns are spiky?
[09:56] Diego: Set min-replicas and keep a warming layer for critical routes; or have a fallback to the bi-encoder score until cross-encoder warms. There's also a gradual rollout approach.
[10:08] Ellen: On storage — do you expose direct S3-compatible storage for vector snapshots?
[10:12] Maya: Yes, snapshots can be exported to S3 buckets and we integrate with customer-managed buckets for Private deployments.
[10:20] [Longer section omitted for brevity: detailed Q/A about index parameters, efConstruction, HNSW in prod, memory per-node estimates and estimated cost math.]
[20:34] Diego: Quick note on recommended index params for HNSW: tune efConstruction at build time and efSearch at query time — higher efSearch gives better recall but higher latency. For 1536 dims we often increase M slightly and provision more memory per shard.
[22:11] Nadia: We're also concerned about GDPR-ish erasure — how do we handle vector deletion and audit trails?
[22:18] Maya: We support per-vector deletion, shredding, and audit logs. For private deployments we can do physical deletion in your AWS account.
[22:30] Tom: One operational question — what's the typical ops load to manage dedicated infra vs hosted? We want minimal ops overhead.
[22:37] Maya: Hosted minimal ops for you but less control; dedicated we still manage the runtime but you get reserved capacity and more configuration; private is most ops. We provide managed support tiers.
[23:00] Ellen: For our bench, expected sample: 1k queries over a 1M vector subset, 1536 dims, using bi-encoder recall + top50 cross-encoder — can you run that?
[23:10] Diego: Yes, we'll run that with quantization profiles and share the traces. We'll include CPU/GPU utilization and batching stats.
[23:18] Nadia: Last question for now — do you have built-in quality monitoring? We need regression alerts when embedding drift occurs.
[23:24] Diego: Redwood Optimize has embedding drift detectors and can run evals against golden prompt sets with alerting. We'll help set up baseline evals.
[23:36] Maya: All right quick recap and next steps: Maya to share SOC2 and cost comparison; Diego to run perf bench and attach traces; HorizonCare to share sample vectors and current schema. Schedule follow-up to review pilot design.
[23:52] Nadia: Sounds good. We'll aim to have sample data by next week.
[23:56] Jacob: Thanks everyone.
[24:00] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links to docs.

Notes about transcription: occasional mislabels: speaker tags may shift; some words like "HNSW" transcribed as "H N S W" in parts; "KMS" sometimes as "K M S". There are a few filler words and clipped sentences.
